items.title: ISC Stormcast For Friday, November 20th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10188, (Fri, Nov 20th)
AI Joins the Industrial Attack Workflow
items.content:
The recent cyberattack on French refrigerators and our tracking of the malicious AI framework ARTEX show that threat actors are increasingly using AI to accelerate attacks, expand their reach, and improve their effectiveness. GreenJuliett, the group behind operational technology (OT) cyberattacks similar to those in France, has begun incorporating AI into its OT attack chain. Understanding the scale AI offers financially motivated and state-sponsored threat actors helps us see it as more than a tool: it’s something that can fill an operator’s role, even while humans remain in control.

On October 11 and 12, 2026, someone changed the defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at more than 700 retail locations in France. This resulted in fires, damaged equipment, and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros, highlighting the physical impacts of attacks against operational technology (OT). On November 9, France attributed the attack to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC). We track activity that likely belongs to an element of Shahid Kaveh as GreenJuliett.

GreenJuliett (also known as CyberAv3ngers and Bauxite) builds infrastructure aimed at internet-facing PLCs. And while that work continued through at least October 30, despite repeated public reporting on the group, the target set began to widen. Between August and October, we observed GreenJuliett-linked infrastructure scanning, or attempting to exploit, Fortinet FortiGate firewalls, edge devices that protect OT networks, in Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. Our network data suggests the group is also working to add internet-of-things (IoT) and CCTV devices to its list.

While we have not independently tied GreenJuliett infrastructure to the refrigeration attacks, over the past three months, we have seen the group continue to target PLCs (programmable logic controllers), which are similar to the internet-exposed controllers the refrigerators in France used. We have also observed that AI is now part of how they work.

From Accounts to Infrastructure

In October 2024, OpenAI banned accounts it assessed as belonging to CyberAv3ngers. The operators had used ChatGPT to research default credentials for PLCs, compile lists of electricity companies and common PLCs in Jordan, and draft scripts against industrial protocols (such as Modbus TCP, a control protocol that allows PLCs to communicate quickly on local networks).

However, in 2026, the picture is different. In October, we found a configuration for LiteLLM (an open-source gateway that puts multiple AI models behind a single interface, suggesting a team-sharing model for access), alongside self-hosted chat applications built for Persian-language users, on infrastructure we assessed as likely used by GreenJuliett-linked operators. We also observed servers in the group's anonymization network communicating with infrastructure that hosts Anthropic's Claude.

While we have not confirmed specific instances of misuse in this research, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported publicly on detecting and disrupting misuse by Iranian government operators. AI shortens the time it takes to identify vulnerable device types and write targeting scripts, and GreenJuliett has moved it from individual accounts into its operating environment.

items.title: Regional Insights: 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
items.content:
Recorded Future’s report surveyed 768 security professionals worldwide on how they use threat intelligence today, how they apply AI to it, and where they plan to invest. The report presents the global findings. The regional executive summaries in this blog cover insights from the same survey, breaking data down by global region into dedicated briefs covering the specific conclusions for cybersecurity leaders in North America, EMEA, APJ, and LATAM. Start with your region to see how your peers are approaching threat intelligence, and read the others for a wider view.

North America (United States and Canada)

In North America, threat intelligence now informs decisions well beyond the security organization. Five teams consume it on average, and 85% of organizations surveyed have teams outside core security using it, including risk management (54%), fraud prevention (44%), and risk and compliance (44%). With intelligence supporting this many teams, 81% plan to invest more in the next 12 months. The challenge is getting the right intelligence to each of those teams in a form they can act on.

Doing that depends on how well intelligence comes together, and this is an ongoing effort for many programs. Most surveyed organizations (63%) draw on four or more intelligence vendors. Only 21% combine that external intelligence with their own internal telemetry in a single platform, where analysts can see which threats apply to their environment. Consolidation plans reflect this. Of the 76% planning to consolidate, the largest share are doing it to improve correlation across signals (40%), compared with only 8% who cite cost.

Moving intelligence from those sources to risk owners is also largely manual. 54% put intelligence into action manually across tools and processes. Among organizations sharing intelligence outside security, 38% rely on ad hoc messages or scheduled reports. Manual handoffs make it harder to see what risk owners did with the intelligence and whether it worked. While 98% measure program value, 28% track whether triggered actions were effective. Only 22% report closed-loop operationalization, where stakeholders act on intelligence, the results are validated, and those results inform the program’s priorities and collection.

AI is already part of this work for nearly all respondents (), and 60% use agents that take actions inside their intelligence tools. Leaders become more cautious as the stakes rise: comfort with letting AI act falls from 71% for summarization to 56% for enforcement actions. The leading barriers are lack of auditability (40%) and unproven accuracy (31%). 73% say intelligence regularly feeds their AI and automation systems or is a core input to them. That makes the quality and correlation of their intelligence a factor in how far they can trust AI to act.

Risk owners can come from procurement, legal, fraud, corporate security, or communications. Threat intelligence innovation means getting the intelligence to the right person to make decisions and take action based on that intelligence.

North America Field CISO at Recorded Future

This summary draws on responses from 347 North American security professionals. They were part of a global survey of 768 that asked how organizations use threat intelligence, apply AI to it, and plan future investments.

The full report covers how intelligence is expanding across the business, what full visibility requires, and what stands between teams and proven impact.

items.title: Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
items.content: <article>About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.</article>
